Slender inshore squid (Doryteuthis pleii) hatchlings emerge from their egg capsules at a remarkably small size, with a neonatal mantle length of just 0.155 cm [Lb = 0.155 cm], a value that has been inferred from studies of the closely related congener Doryteuthis sanpaulensis. This diminutive size at hatching, characteristic of many loliginid squids, implies an extended vulnerability during the early planktonic phase, during which the paralarvae must locate and capture suitable prey to fuel rapid growth. Experimental work conducted under controlled thermal conditions has shown that at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C], the period between oviposition and hatching spans approximately 10.5 days [ab = approximately 10.5 days], a brief embryonic duration that is consistent with the elevated metabolic rates typical of cephalopod development at such temperatures. This rapid developmental pace, coupled with the small size at which individuals begin exogenous feeding, is a hallmark of the species' opportunistic life-history strategy in the subtropical waters it inhabits along the southwestern Atlantic coast.

As growth proceeds through the juvenile and sub-adult stages, the timing of sexual maturation exhibits a marked sexual dimorphism that is reflected in size at puberty. Both sexes undergo gonadal activation when they reach a mantle length of 14.33 cm [Lp = 14.33 cm], a common developmental benchmark that initiates gametogenesis and the onset of reproductive capability. However, males experience a considerable delay in reaching functional maturity as defined by the completion of spermatophore production, which typically occurs only after they attain a mantle length of 21.0 cm [Lp = 21.0 cm]. This divergence suggests that male reproductive success may be more tightly linked to body size, likely because larger males have a competitive advantage in the context of intersexual selection and territorial disputes over access to spawning grounds. The protracted period of somatic growth before achieving full male maturity likely reflects the energetic demands associated with developing the relatively large hectocotylus and complex spermatophoric organs required for successful copulation.

The maximum mantle length attained by reproductively active individuals of Doryteuthis pleii also differs substantially between the sexes, a pattern commonly observed in many cephalopod species with a semelparous terminal spawning strategy. Females, which invest heavily in the production of large, yolk-rich eggs and have a relatively compressed post-spawning lifespan, generally reach a maximum dorsal mantle length of 22.0 cm [Li = 22.0 cm] at the time of death. In contrast, males continue to grow for a longer period and achieve a considerably larger terminal size, with a recorded maximum mantle length of 33.0 cm [Li = 33.0 cm] at death. This pronounced sexual size dimorphism, where males are nearly fifty percent larger than females at the end of their lives, is thought to be driven by intense male-male competition for mating opportunities, a dynamic that favors larger body size despite the inherently high metabolic costs of sustaining such growth in a short-lived, fast-growing lineage.

All major life-history milestones in this species appear tightly coupled to the prevailing thermal regime, with laboratory and field observations converging on a reference temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C] for establishing typical developmental rates. Just prior to the final spawning event, the gonadosomatic index (GSI) of female Doryteuthis pleii reached a peak value of 13% [GSI = 13%] at a water temperature of 16 °C [T = 16 °C]. This parameter, which expresses the proportional contribution of ovarian mass to total body mass, indicates that the ovaries constitute roughly thirteen percent of the female's somatic weight at the moment of reproductive culmination. The energetic cost of this final reproductive event is catastrophic, triggering a rapid failure of physiological homeostasis and a cessation of all vital functions, a pattern that underscores the extreme trade-off between current reproductive output and any residual capacity for future survival.
